Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Panama Canal Authority runs daily auctions that allow ship owners to place bids to skip the queue. Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images Shipping industry Panama canal fees soar due to Iran war and El Niño as ship ‘pays $4m to jump queue’ Falling water levels linked to weather system are expected to limit number of slots to transit shipping lane Business live – latest updates Joanna Partridge Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.26 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Commercial ships travelling through the Panama canal are facing a rise in costs amid disruption triggered by the Iran war and falling water levels linked to this year’s intense El Niño weather system . Highlighting the fragility of global trade, a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump a queue of vessels waiting to pass through the vital maritime choke point. Ships are now waiting about 10 days for their turn to pass through the trade route linking the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, the largest backlog since May, according to Argus Media. The route is favoured by shippers as it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for large retailers and energy companies that trade between Asia and the US. ‘Like being in prison’: the ship crews stuck in Gulf since February Read more While shipping companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP), which manages the waterway, also runs daily auctions that allow shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Starting bids open at about $15,000 for smaller cargo vessels and $55,000 for the largest ships, but these prices can shoot up during times of heavy congestion or high demand. The buyer of the $4m transit slot was reported to be the Seaspan Benefactor, a 10,100 TEU (20-foot equivalent unit) vessel, according to Bloomberg. The payment was reportedly more than double the average bid placed during the previous seven days. Shipowners are willing to pay significantly higher prices at auction to avoid queues, as more vessels stay away from the Gulf and the Red Sea as fighting in the Middle East has effectively closed the strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab , the narrow waterway between the Arabian peninsula and the Horn of Africa. Prices to travel in the Panama canal’s busiest shipping lanes have hit record highs, according to the Financial Times, at a time when water levels are falling amid the rapidly developing El Niño weather system . Earlier this month the ACP said it would impose limits in late August and early September on how low vessels can travel through the water, known as a ship’s draft, in an effort to keep traffic flowing. The authority had also cut the maximum authorised draft in July, in a measure forcing ships transiting its Neopanamax locks – the canal’s wider and deeper lane – to carry lighter cargoes. The decision was based on water levels and projected conditions for Gatun Lake, an artificial reservoir that feeds the canal, the ACP said, adding it was “ready to implement preventive measures” during El Niño based on lessons learned during the event in 2023-4 and as it monitors weather conditions. Some shipowners are concerned the ACP could introduce restrictions on the number of vessels allowed to transit the waterway, as in 2023 when a lengthy drought in the central American country led to a logjam. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion It comes after the ACP recorded a 5% increase in the number of transits between October and June, representing an average of 35 a day. A higher tonnage was carried through the canal during this period, with the increase driven by container ships and liquefied petroleum gas carriers, the ACP said. The Panama canal is not the only crucial trade route affected by low water levels, amid growing international concern over the economic consequences of the climate emergency. A prolonged period of dry weather across Europe has led to record low water levels on the Rhine, with traders warning that it was not possible to book some cargo shipments on the river, forcing them to pay higher costs to transport goods by road and rail instead. The Rhine is one of Europe’s main arteries for transporting grain, fuel, minerals and goods, but manufacturers have had to reduce the amount of cargo transported on ships as a result of the low water levels. https://www.dw.com/en/could-ukraine-s-my.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JFV2 Mykhailo Fedorov in the video address he published on his YouTube channel on August 18 Image: Mykhailo Fedorov/YouTube/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement This past week, Ukraine was rocked by a series of political scandals. A month after stepping down as defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov addressed the Ukrainian people in a nine-minute speech posted on his YouTube channel. In his video message, he declares that Ukraine "cannot remain without a fully appointed minister of defense." But, he continues, "the main problem goes much deeper than one position or one ministry." He says Ukraine's greatest challenge is a "systemic crisis of governance," of which corruption is only a symptom. Fedorov also criticized the fact that no national elections have been held in Ukraine since 2019. A few hours earlier, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , had proposed Yevhenii Khmara to parliament as the new defense minister. Khmara had been made acting minister of defense on July 20, and parliament confirmed him in the position on August 19. Yevhenii Khmara attends a session of the Ukrainian parliament on August 19, when he was appointed minister of defense Image: REUTERS Ukraine corruption scandal involves high-ranking officials When Fedorov spoke of corruption in government authorities, he may not have known about the scandal that would break the very day after he published his speech. On August 19, Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators searched the premises of several high-ranking officials, including a presidential deputy chief of staff, Iryna Mudra, and a member of parliament, Vadym Stolar. Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) stated that it was "conducting a special operation to expose a criminal organization" in conjunction with the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office. According to the investigating authorities, this organization was led by a current and a former Ukrainian lawmaker, and involved senior officials from the president's office. Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mudra from her post as presidential deputy chief of staff the same day. In his video, Mykhailo Fedorov warns that "it is especially dangerous when society feels that the main criterion for appointing a person is not their professionalism, results, or ability […] but their personal loyalty to the system." He says that a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism" needs to be found to make it possible to hold elections, even if Russia's war against Ukraine continues for a long time. Why is Fedorov's support growing in Ukraine? The president dismissed Fedorov from his post as defense minister on July 15. Protests calling for his reinstatement began the following day in Kyiv, Lviv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and other cities. According to polls conducted by the Rating opinion research institute on July 20 and 21, trust in the ex-minister rose from 35% to 65% in the first week of the protests. Of the respondents, 72% thought Fedorov should not have been sacked. Thousands demonstrated in cities around Ukraine to protest the dismissal of Fedorov as defense minister Image: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/picture alliance A poll conducted on August 5 and 6 showed Fedorov in third place in the presidential ratings, on 12.5%. Volodymyr Zelenskyy led with 25.2%, followed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian army, on 16.7%. Ihor Chalenko, a political scientist from the Center for Analysis and Strategies in Kyiv, says Fedorov's address was an attempt to consolidate the political capital he won during the protests. Even though Fedorov does not present a full election program in his video, Chalenko thinks he is calculating on positioning himself as an independent political player who could stand against Volodymyr Zelenskyy. "For 35 days, people were out on the street. The demonstrations started with the demand that Fedorov be reinstated as minister of defense. But the fear is that the spotlight has moved on from Fedorov, because the protest campaign became increasingly focused on the fight against corruption and protecting the anti-corruption authorities. So the former minister has decided to position himself politically and secure the status he attained," Chalenko said in an interview with DW. Is Fedorov positioning himself against Zelenskyy? However, Chalenko doesn't believe that Fedorov has shifted to "irreconcilable opposition" to Zelenskyy. While there is clearly a conflict between Fedorov and the president's inner circle, Chalenko doesn't see this as a permanent rift with the government, and he doesn't rule out a return for Fedorov were he to be offered a position. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet been directly challenged as the constitution forbids elections in wartime Image: Ukrainian Presidentia/Planet Pix via ZUMA Press Wire/dpa/picture alliance Oleksiy Haran, a professor of political science at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy, thinks Fedorov's remarks about elections and a renewal of the power of state send an important signal. However, he too says he sees no decisive change in opposition to the president. "We haven't heard any criticism at all of Zelenskyy," he told DW. What would Ukraine need to hold wartime elections? Haran says Fedorov's speech expresses what the people want. Polls show that Ukrainians do indeed want a change of government. However, the political scientist emphasizes that there is a problem: "We agree that Russia cannot dictate to us when and how we should hold elections. But the question is: how should we hold elections if Russia continues the war?" He believes that in order to hold full elections a stable ceasefire is needed, at the very least, and this is precisely what Fedorov does not mention in his remarks. Vadym Denysenko, a political analyst at the Ukrainian thinktank Business Capital, believes Fedorov's speech is not an election campaign by one former minister but the start of a bigger political game. In a Facebook post, Denysenko describes two developments he is observing one month after Fedorov's dismissal. First, the social milieu he refers to as "Self-Help 3.0", which includes the anti-corruption movement, has found a political leader in Fedorov. Secondly, some of Zelenskyy's former followers have switched allegiance to Fedorov, and these, the analyst says, are now his strongest supporters. Denysenko appreciates Fedorov's comments as a contribution to the discussion about renewing the power of state. He points out that these are the same ideas Zelenskyy campaigned on in 2019. Even though Fedorov doesn't directly say in his video that he would stand in an election, the analyst is sure this is what Fedorov's inner circle is working toward. And, in his view, they have nothing to lose. "If elections were to be held soon, Fedorov stands a good chance of doing well," Denysenko says. "If there are no elections, they can strengthen his grassroots support, and further weaken Zelenskyy." This article was originally published in Ukrainian. Set us as your Preferred Source on Google By Rebecca Henrys Germany is in touch with Romania over the possible extradition of a man detained there in connection with a gun stash found in a forest near Berlin last year, said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Friday. "This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level," said Dobrindt at a press conference. He described the suspect as a "low-level agent" without knowledge of the line of command steering him, adding that several similarly uninformed operatives had been detained so far this year, including one Kazakh national. While earlier media reports by Sueddeutsche Zeitung and other outlets quoted sources as saying that German intelligence believes the weapons were meant to be used for assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence, the minister only said he could not rule out the involvement of foreign powers. Read more: 'I understand why people feel angry about this' Andy Burnham weighs in on rise of smart glasses - but fails to commit to ban Read more: Tate brothers referred to counter-terror police over alleged Russia propaganda trip Dobrindt said the suspect, whose nationality he would not disclose, was also held in connection with planned parcel bomb attacks in Romania. This would play a role in talks with Romanian authorities over a potential extradition. "We will then determine, in the course of the investigation, what measures can be taken against this person," he added. Romania's justice ministry did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Dobrindt said the stash, which also included ammunition, was placed under surveillance for months after its discovery but nobody was seen approaching it. By Laura Gozzi Â and Â Olga Malchevska Published 30 October 2026, 10:32 GMT Updated 47 minutes ago The evacuation of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky is under way, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have confirmed. A ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined. The residents of Oleshky who wish to leave have a four-hour window to do so. An evacuation convoy of 25 buses will allow up to 750 people to leave Oleshky until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility. It is understood several hundred people have decided to stay in the town, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water. "Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said. "At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance." Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa. They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region. Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Russian sappers have been demining the road out of Oleshky since Tuesday Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday. Lantratova later posted a video on social media from the town, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine. In videos posted by his own social media account, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive." Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators. An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it." Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind. "The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise." Her grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter. "She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said. "That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows." The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
